5	// Kimi is an adapter target, not a second tier resolver -- same posture as codex.js.
6	// Keep the conceptual Claude-like tiers in model.js; translate only when emitting
7	// Kimi config. Evidence: docs/research/kimi-code-cli.md section 11 (2026-07-23,
8	// Moonshot platform docs + AA/DeepSWE/vendor benchmarks).
9	//
10	// Model ids are the Kimi Code config ALIASES a live install resolves (`kimi -m
11	// <alias>` / default_model), NOT raw platform API ids. Grounded in the actual
12	// managed Kimi Code plan (~/.kimi-code/config.toml, 2026-07-23): it serves three
13	// coding models -- kimi-code/k3, kimi-code/kimi-for-coding, and
14	// kimi-code/kimi-for-coding-highspeed -- and ALL THREE are always-thinking (the
15	// managed coding plan exposes no non-thinking or cheaper general model; k2.6/k2.5
16	// are Open-Platform general models on a different endpoint, not offered here).
17	//
18	// The two constraints Kimi imposes that Codex/Claude do not:
19	// - Reasoning EFFORT exists on K3 ONLY, and is 3 rungs: low | high | max (default
20	//   high on the managed plan). kimi-for-coding[-highspeed] expose NO effort field
21	//   -- always-thinking, no knob. So a semantic effort override only bites on the
22	//   two K3 tiers; on sonnet/haiku it is a documented no-op.
23	// - muster's medium/xhigh efforts are not native. Kimi's ladder collapses them
24	//   (medium -> high, xhigh -> max), so workhorse and judgment both land on high.
25	//
26	// Per-lane rationale (reconciled to what the managed plan actually installs):
27	// - haiku  = kimi-for-coding: the dedicated coding model, the SAME lane as sonnet.
28	//   The managed coding plan has no cheaper/general model (no k2.6/k2.5 -- the
29	//   research's cheap locator lane does not exist on this endpoint), so read-only
30	//   locate/gather rides the same model as the build workhorse. NEVER highspeed:
31	//   kimi-for-coding-highspeed is the IDENTICAL K2.7 model that merely burns ~3x
32	//   the plan usage to trade for latency -- pointing the "cheap" read-only lane at
33	//   a 3x-cost SKU of the same model would be exactly backwards, so muster never
34	//   spends quota there. haiku and sonnet therefore resolve identically on Kimi;
35	//   the tier split survives at model.js for routing/budget/degradation, mirroring
36	//   Codex's fable->opus collapse. Confirmed by a live GET /v1/models probe
37	//   (2026-07-24, HTTP 200): the plan serves EXACTLY {kimi-for-coding,
38	//   kimi-for-coding-highspeed, k3, k3-256k}, all supports_thinking_type "only" --
39	//   no cheaper family exists to remap to. `muster install kimi --probe` re-runs
40	//   that check (src/kimi-install.js probeKimiModels) and would flag a genuinely
41	//   cheaper alias IF the plan ever gains one.
42	// - sonnet = kimi-for-coding: the dedicated coding workhorse. Always-thinking.
43	// - opus   = k3, effort high: the judgment lane. K3 is frontier and holds quality
44	//   to 1M context (BrowseComp 90.4 @ 1M). high = the plan's default judgment effort.
45	// - fable  = k3, effort max: same model, max reserved to the rare peak only -- the
46	//   discipline Codex applies to xhigh. K3's effort knob gives a cleaner opus/fable
47	//   split than Codex (where both are sol/high).
48	//
49	// A tier entry carries EITHER `effort` (a K3 reasoning level) OR `thinking` (the
50	// always-on toggle for the effort-less coding models).
51	const KIMI_TIERS = Object.freeze({
52	  haiku: Object.freeze({ model: "kimi-code/kimi-for-coding", thinking: "enabled" }),
53	  sonnet: Object.freeze({ model: "kimi-code/kimi-for-coding", thinking: "enabled" }),
54	  opus: Object.freeze({ model: "kimi-code/k3", effort: "high" }),
55	  fable: Object.freeze({ model: "kimi-code/k3", effort: "max" }),
56	});
57	
58	// Semantic effort -> Kimi K3 reasoning level. K3's native ladder is 3 rungs, so
59	// workhorse and judgment both resolve to `high` (K3 has no `medium`) and peak to
60	// `max` -- the same aliasing Kimi Code applies to third-party effort inputs.
61	const KIMI_EFFORT = Object.freeze({
62	  workhorse: "high",
63	  judgment: "high",
64	  peak: "max",
65	});
66	
67	export const KIMI_MODEL_POLICY = Object.freeze({
68	  tiers: KIMI_TIERS,
69	  // A semantic effort override only applies where the resolved model exposes an
70	  // effort knob (K3). On an always-thinking model (kimi-for-coding[-highspeed])
71	  // it is intentionally a no-op: Kimi gives no way to dial reasoning there.
72	  applyEffort(base, semantic) {
73	    if (!("effort" in base)) return base;
74	    return { ...base, effort: KIMI_EFFORT[semantic] ?? base.effort };
75	  },
76	});
77	
78	export function kimiModelForTier(tier) {
79	  const resolved = KIMI_MODEL_POLICY.tiers[tier];
80	  if (!resolved) throw new Error(`unknown Muster model tier: ${tier}`);
81	  return { ...resolved };
82	}
83	
84	// --- The two-lane dispatch bind (model_preference) ---------------------------
85	//
86	// Kimi DOES support a per-agent model selector -- it is just not Claude Code's
87	// `model:` field (which Kimi explicitly ignores). An agent file carries
88	// `model_preference: primary | secondary`, where (docs, customization/agents):
89	// "`primary` selects the caller's main model, while `secondary` selects
90	// `[secondary_model] model`". `[secondary_model]` is "a second model pointer
91	// next to the primary `default_model`" in config.toml, carrying its own `model`
92	// and `default_effort`.
93	//
94	// So Kimi gives TWO models per launch, selectable per agent -- not the "one
95	// model per launch" the earlier research recorded. muster's four conceptual
96	// tiers fold onto those two lanes along the family line KIMI_TIERS already
97	// draws: the K3 judgment family and the K2.7 Coding execution family.
98	//
99	//   primary   = kimi-code/k3               <- opus + fable
100	//   secondary = kimi-code/kimi-for-coding  <- haiku + sonnet
101	//
102	// fable collapses into opus's lane (both k3, but effort is per-launch, not
103	// per-agent) -- the SAME degradation Codex already accepts, where fable and opus
104	// are both sol/high. Nothing new is lost.
105	//
106	// Two constraints on using this (both are the caller's job, not this map's):
107	//  1. It is EXPERIMENTAL and off by default -- `KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_SECONDARY_MODEL=1`
108	//     under `kimi web`, or `KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FLAG=1` under `kimi -p`.
109	//     The interactive TUI "currently ignores this field".
110	//  2. The mapping is only CORRECT if config.toml's default_model/[secondary_model]
111	//     match KIMI_LANES below -- muster emits that block for the user rather than
112	//     mutating a shared config itself (see src/kimi-install.js).
113	//
114	// Omitting the field is NOT neutral: per the docs, when a secondary model is
115	// configured and an agent omits model_preference, "the configured secondary
116	// model remains the default" -- i.e. every un-annotated agent silently binds to
117	// the CHEAP lane, judgment agents included. That is precisely why the install
118	// stamps this field on every agent instead of copying files through untouched.
119	export const KIMI_LANES = Object.freeze({
120	  primary: "kimi-code/k3",
121	  secondary: "kimi-code/kimi-for-coding"
122	});
123	
124	// Derived from KIMI_TIERS (never a parallel hand-maintained table): a tier's
125	// lane is whichever KIMI_LANES entry names the same model its tier resolves to.
126	// A tier whose model matches no lane fails loud rather than guessing a lane.
127	export function kimiModelPreferenceForTier(tier) {
128	  const { model } = kimiModelForTier(tier);
129	  const lane = Object.keys(KIMI_LANES).find(name => KIMI_LANES[name] === model);
130	  if (!lane) throw new Error(`Kimi tier ${tier} resolves to ${model}, which is not a configured lane`);
131	  return lane;
132	}
133	
134	// Resolve an agent id (a manifest key) to its Kimi lane. Returns null for an id
135	// with no manifest entry -- the caller decides whether that is a skip or a fault.
136	export function kimiPreferenceForAgentId(id) {
137	  const config = agentProfiles()[id];
138	  return config ? kimiModelPreferenceForTier(config.tier) : null;
139	}
140	
141	// --- The runtime lane bind (single source of truth) --------------------------
142	//
143	// The stamped model_preference lanes engage only when the secondary-model
144	// experiment is on for the PROCESS (docs/research/kimi-code-cli.md section 11.8):
145	//   KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FLAG=1   selects the v2 engine under `kimi -p`,
146	//                                   which is what makes model_preference bite
147	//   KIMI_SECONDARY_MODEL=<alias>    points the secondary lane at a model
148	// Both are per-process, so binding this way mutates nothing in the user's
149	// shared config.toml and leaves interactive sessions untouched (the TUI ignores
150	// model_preference anyway -- lanes bind under `kimi -p` / `kimi web` only).
151	//
152	// Both values are DERIVED here from the tier map, never re-stated by callers:
153	// the lane models are whatever the judgment (opus) and execution (sonnet)
154	// families resolve to, checked against KIMI_LANES so a hand edit that drifts
155	// the two apart fails loud instead of silently binding the wrong lane. Every
156	// Kimi spawn path shares this one derivation -- kimiGoalInvocation
157	// (src/kimi-dispatch.js) for the live `kimi -p` run loop, the install report
158	// (src/kimi-install.js), and `muster doctor` (src/doctor.js).
159	export function kimiLaneBinding() {
160	  const primary = kimiModelForTier("opus").model;    // the K3 judgment family
161	  const secondary = kimiModelForTier("sonnet").model; // the K2.7 Coding execution family
162	  if (KIMI_LANES.primary !== primary || KIMI_LANES.secondary !== secondary) {
163	    throw new Error(`KIMI_LANES drifted from KIMI_TIERS: lanes name ${KIMI_LANES.primary} / ${KIMI_LANES.secondary}, but the tiers resolve ${primary} / ${secondary}`);
164	  }
165	  const tiers = {};
166	  for (const tier of Object.keys(KIMI_TIERS)) tiers[tier] = kimiModelPreferenceForTier(tier);
167	  return {
168	    lanes: { primary, secondary },
169	    tiers,
170	    env: {
171	      KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FLAG: "1",
172	      KIMI_SECONDARY_MODEL: secondary
173	    }
174	  };
175	}
176	
177	// Just the env pair, for spawn sites that need nothing else. Returns a fresh
178	// object each call -- a caller mutating it must not corrupt the next spawn.
179	export function kimiLaneEnv() {
180	  return { ...kimiLaneBinding().env };
181	}
182	
183	// Adapter boundary for callers that resolve a role at runtime. modelForRole keeps
184	// MUSTER_MAX_TIER and Fable's deterministic fallback (fable -> opus when Fable is
185	// disabled), so a fable-set role with Fable off resolves to the opus (k3/high)
186	// profile, and with MUSTER_ENABLE_FABLE to the fable (k3/max) profile.
187	export function kimiModelForRole(role) {
188	  return kimiModelForTier(modelForRole(role));
189	}
190	
191	// SINGLE SOURCE for the concrete Kimi profile a HARNESS-NEUTRAL agent config
192	// resolves to. Consumes { tier, effort? } (model-policy.js) -- no concrete model
193	// strings -- so the same manifest entry resolves on Codex, Kimi, and Claude alike.
194	// Mirrors codexProfileForConfig's role in the Codex adapter.
195	export function kimiProfileForConfig(config) {
196	  return resolveNeutralProfile(config, KIMI_MODEL_POLICY);
197	}
198	
199	// Resolve an agent id (a `capabilities --kimi` chosen.id == a manifest agent key)
200	// to its concrete Kimi profile {model, effort|thinking}, from the SHARED
201	// harness-neutral manifest (agent-manifest.js reads catalog/agents.manifest.json
202	// -- the SAME file codex.js resolves). Returns null for a non-agent provider
203	// (skill/mcp/inline) with no manifest entry. Mirrors codexProfileForAgentId.
204	export function kimiProfileForAgentId(id) {
205	  const config = agentProfiles()[id];
206	  return config ? kimiProfileForConfig(config) : null;
207	}

1	# Kimi Code CLI — harness internals, implementation-grade
2	
3	Research for a candidate muster harness binding, gathered 2026-07-23 from Moonshot AI's own
4	docs (`www.kimi.com/code/docs`, `moonshotai.github.io/kimi-code`, `www.kimi-cli.com`), the
5	DeepWiki index of `MoonshotAI/kimi-cli`, PyPI, and the Moonshot Open Platform pricing pages.
6	Same frame as `codex-cli.md` and `hermes.md`: reduce the harness to the six primitives
7	`docs/binding-interface.md` defines (Dispatch, Ask, Enforce, Isolate, Receipts, Capability
8	scan), bind each to its exact Kimi mechanism, and state the degradation ladder. Capability tags
9	below use the `kc-` prefix, parallel to `cc-`/`cx-`/`hermes-` in
10	`docs/research/reference-harness-design.md`.
11	
12	**Headline.** Of every non-Anthropic harness muster has evaluated, Kimi Code is the closest
13	structural clone of Claude Code — deliberately so. It ships `Agent`/`AgentSwarm` subagent
14	dispatch, a Claude-Code-format agent-`.md` loader, a near-1:1 hook lifecycle, an
15	`SKILL.md`-convention skill system, a plugin marketplace with a readable on-disk registry, and
16	even a built-in `/import-from-cc-codex` skill. Four of the six primitives bind **natively**;
17	only Isolate drops to the Codex floor, and Ask is native-shaped-but-narrow. The single real
18	friction for muster is model routing: gen2 has **no per-subagent model and no fast/router
19	tier** — the tier→model map resolves to one model per launch, not per role.
20	
21	---
22	
23	## 0. Two generations — keep them separate
24	
25	`kimi` is the command name for **two distinct products from the same team**. Muster targets
26	gen2; gen1 is winding down but its docs are more complete on shared internals, so it is the
27	better source for how the agent loop actually works.
28	
29	| | **Gen1 — `kimi-cli`** | **Gen2 — Kimi Code CLI (`kimi-code`)** |
30	|---|---|---|
31	| Language | Python ≥3.12 | TypeScript on Node.js ≥22.19 |
32	| Distribution | PyPI `kimi-cli` (v1.49.0, 2026-07-16)

605	Two deliberate design calls:
606	
607	- **Which lane is primary.** K3 primary / K2.7 secondary means an un-annotated agent fails
608	  *cheap*. Inverting it (K2.7 primary) would give better orchestrator quota but make an
609	  un-annotated third-party agent default to frontier K3. Fail-cheap wins.
610	- **muster does not write the MODEL half of `config.toml`.** It is a shared, user-owned file, and the
611	  hook-bombardment diagnosis is the standing lesson on muster mutating shared harness config. The
612	  install *reports* the required delta (`modelPreference.requiredConfig`) and leaves the edit to the
613	  user. Declining it is safe: with no secondary model configured, every agent inherits the caller's
614	  model and the stamps are inert. The **preferred** route is the per-process env pair
615	  `KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FLAG=1` + `KIMI_SECONDARY_MODEL=kimi-code/kimi-for-coding`, which binds
616	  the lanes for a muster-launched `kimi -p` while mutating nothing and leaving the user's
617	  interactive sessions untouched. (`KIMI_SECONDARY_EFFORT` sets the lane's effort.) The ONE
618	  exception to "no config writes" (since 2026-07-26): `muster install kimi` merges a
619	  marker-delimited `[[permission.rules]]` deny block (the action-class fence, §4.2) into
620	  `config.toml` — a pure add/remove of muster's own block, never an edit of the user's settings.

622	The gate is not optional: `model_preference` "applies only to newly spawned subagents when the
623	secondary-model experiment is enabled", and **"The TUI currently ignores this field."** Lanes bind
624	under `kimi -p` / `kimi web`, never in the interactive TUI. An explicit `model: "primary"|"secondary"`
625	on the `Agent`/`AgentSwarm` *call* overrides the profile — so muster can also tier per dispatch, not
626	just per profile (it is "ignored when resuming"; resumed subagents keep their model).

649	### 11.9 Native dispatch — AgentSwarm + `/goal` (2026-07-25)

FAIL
BLOCKER: The outcome claims the stamped `model_preference` on the `--agent-file` agent engages the `-p` process's own model lanes; `model_preference` only selects `primary`/`secondary` for subagents spawned by that agent when `KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FLAG=1` and `KIMI_SECONDARY_MODEL` are set, not for the main `-p` agent.
BLOCKER: The outcome claims the dispatch "needs no `-m` flag"; the harness always emits `-m <lane>` because the `-p` main agent's model comes only from `-m`, and omitting it silently falls back to `config.toml`'s `default_model` (`kimi-code/k3`), demoting execution-lane work onto the judgment lane.
BLOCKER: The `dispatch` string `"kimi -p --agent-file muster-reviewer.md"` omits the required `-p` prompt/brief, the mandatory `-m` lane flag, and the `--output-format stream-json` the harness uses; the actual descriptor is `[-p, brief, --agent-file, path, --output-format, stream-json, -m, KIMI_LANES[lane]]`.
BLOCKER: The manifest omits the per-process env pair; the harness merges `KIMI_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_FLAG=1` and `KIMI_SECONDARY_MODEL=kimi-code/kimi-for-coding` over the ambient env on every spawn, so without it the stamped lanes are inert.
MINOR: "the `-p` process's own model lanes" implies plural lanes per process; a single `-p` process has one main model (`-m`) and only its spawned subagents get a lane via `model_preference`.
MINOR: The manifest conflates the agent-file stamp with dispatch argv; the harness keeps install-time stamping (`kimiPreferenceForAgentId` → `model_preference`) separate from runtime lane enforcement (`-m` + env pair).
